title: Multiple-feature linear regression
description: Two input features, three parameters and two complete batch updates.
source: Lecture 1 - Introduction.pdf, pages 43-44; Home work 1 on Linear Regression.docx.

pages.title: Two inputs, one prediction
pages.subtitle: Each example has two measured features. It still has one target.
blocks: Lecture 1, page 43. The dot product multiplies matching components and adds them. T means transpose.
x0 = 1 is bookkeeping for the bias, not a third measured feature. Parameter order throughout: (b, w1, w2).

pages.title: Start with three zero parameters
pages.subtitle: Feature subscripts choose columns; example superscripts choose rows.
blocks: Residual r is prediction minus target. J is half-MSE, matching Lecture 1.

pages.title: One gradient for every parameter
pages.subtitle: Differentiate the same loss with respect to each parameter separately.

blocks.eq: \frac{\partial r_i}{\partial b}=1,\quad\frac{\partial r_i}{\partial w_1}=x_1^{(i)},\quad\frac{\partial r_i}{\partial w_2}=x_2^{(i)}

blocks: The square derivative contributes 2r; 2 cancels 1/2. Multiply by the relevant input through the chain rule.

blocks.eq: g_b=\frac{\sum_i r_i}{m},\quad g_1=\frac{\sum_i r_ix_1^{(i)}}{m},\quad g_2=\frac{\sum_i r_ix_2^{(i)}}{m}

blocks: Lecture 1, page 44: bias is the same rule with x0 = 1. Average each column once.

pages.title: First step: calculate all contributions
pages.subtitle: Each row contributes (residual, residual times x1, residual times x2).
blocks: A zero input makes that example contribute zero to that weight gradient, even if its prediction is wrong.

pages.title: First simultaneous update
pages.subtitle: Use the same old parameter vector for all three right-hand sides.
blocks: Store the three new values, then replace the old ones together. One pass over all three examples produced one full-batch update.

pages.title: Recompute after the first update
pages.subtitle: The second iteration must start with fresh predictions and residuals.
blocks: The cost fell from 2.333333 to 0.51. Do not reuse the initial residuals.

pages.title: Second step: contributions and means
pages.subtitle: Again, the order in every triple is (bias, weight 1, weight 2).
blocks: The second example is exactly predicted, so its current contribution is zero.

pages.title: Second update and new predictions
pages.subtitle: Each parameter has its own gradient, but the learning rate is shared.

pages.title: Verify the second cost
pages.subtitle: The middle example gets worse, but the average fit still improves.
blocks: These are costs at initialization, after update 1, and after update 2.
Shared parameters create tradeoffs across examples. A smaller mean cost does not guarantee improvement for each point.

pages.title: Connect this to Homework 1
pages.subtitle: The homework uses the same rules with six rows and learning rate 0.01.
blocks: Homework 1 starts w1 = w2 = b = 0. Its first data row is (x1, x2, y) = (1, 2, 11).
This is only the FIRST ROW contribution, not the full gradient. Repeat for all six rows, sum each column and divide by 6.
Then update all three parameters using alpha = 0.01. Our three-row toy data and alpha = 0.3 are study choices, not the homework dataset.
Common mistakes: confusing a feature index with an example index; forgetting the bias; mixing parameter order.

pages.title: Your turn: a negative feature value
pages.subtitle: Use one example so you can check every multiplication by hand.
blocks: Calculate the prediction, signed residual, and three gradients.
Update all parameters simultaneously. Recompute the prediction and half-MSE.
Pay special attention to the sign of the weight 2 gradient.

pages.title: Practice answer: one full update
pages.subtitle: The negative input reverses the sign of its weight contribution.
